content: Rheumatic heart disease continues to be a significant cause of acquired heart disease in developing countries. While the prevention of rheumatic fever and the management of its recurrences are well-established, the optimal treatment for active rheumatic carditis remains uncertain. This review updates previous versions published in 2003, 2009, and 2012. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects—both beneficial and harmful—of anti-inflammatory agents, including aspirin, corticosteroids, and other drugs, in preventing or reducing further valvular damage in patients with acute rheumatic fever. To gather relevant data, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, covering studies up to October 2013. No language restrictions were applied. Additionally, reference lists of identified studies were reviewed. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing anti-inflammatory agents (e.g., aspirin, corticosteroids, immunoglobulins, pentoxifylline) with placebo, no treatment, or other anti-inflammatory agents were included. The primary outcome was the presence of cardiac disease one year after treatment. Two authors independently extracted data and assessed the risk of bias using Cochrane's standardized methodology. Eight RCTs involving 996 participants were included in the review. These trials compared various corticosteroids (e.g., corticotrophin, cortisone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, prednisone) and intravenous immunoglobulin with aspirin, placebo, or no treatment. Six of these trials were conducted between 1950 and 1965, one in 1990, and the most recent in 2001. The results showed no significant differences in the risk of cardiac disease at one year between corticosteroid-treated and aspirin-treated groups (six studies, 907 participants; risk ratio [RR] 0.87, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.66 to 1.15). Similarly, prednisone use (two studies, 212 participants; RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.52 to 2.45) did not reduce the risk of heart disease compared to aspirin. Adverse events were not reported in five studies, while three studies documented substantial adverse events. However, the findings must be interpreted cautiously due to the age of the studies and the high risk of bias. The authors concluded that there is little evidence to support the use of corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulins in reducing the risk of heart valve lesions in patients with acute rheumatic fever. The outdated nature of most trials limited the ability to perform robust statistical analyses and assess clinical outcomes by modern standards. Furthermore, the substantial risk of bias in the included studies necessitates caution in interpreting the results. The authors emphasized the need for new RCTs to evaluate the effects of corticosteroids, such as oral prednisone and intravenous methylprednisolone, as well as other novel anti-inflammatory agents. Advances in echocardiography could facilitate more objective and precise assessments of cardiac outcomes in future studies.
